Jaya, you're panicking about the Onam release, so let your Hemant Uncle tell you about mine. Fifteen years ago I was your age, twenty-four, and our boss wanted a small booking app out before Onam.
I sat down with a pencil. Onam was the second of September. Before release, the store check. Before that, testing. Before that, the booking screen, and that depended on the payment screen, which depended on the login. I wrote it all as a chain on one sheet and pinned it by the tea machine for the whole team.
Then my senior, old Krishnan, made me do one more thing. "Now pull every date two weeks earlier," he said. I argued. He won.
And good thing. The payment company changed its rules in August. We lost eleven days. We still launched on the twentieth.
So take your dates, beta, and give them room to breathe.

Dear Kunal,
I know you think I'm being gloomy, but hear me out before Friday's fest.
Last night I tried something. I pretended it was Saturday and our bookmark stall had completely flopped. Then I asked myself: why did it flop? I wrote down whatever came.
1. People paid with big notes and we had no change, so they walked off.
2. It rained, and paper bookmarks got soggy.
3. We got the corner behind the stage where nobody walks.
None of these were in our plan. Our plan was only colours and prices!
So can you bring a bag of ten-rupee notes and coins from your dad's shop? I'll get plastic sleeves and a tarp. And let's ask Mrs Pillai tomorrow if we can swap for a spot near the food stalls.
Not gloomy. Just ready.
Keerthana

I'm Rekha, and last winter I wanted to start a tiffin delivery service for students in our area.
A mentor told me to do a pre-mortem: imagine it has failed and list why. So I did, on a Sunday night. Cooks quit. Food goes bad. Hostel bans outside food. Scooter breaks down. Payment app fails. Students go home for holidays. Competitor opens. Rent rises. I didn't stop. By two in the morning I had fifty-three reasons across four pages.
I read them in a row and felt sick. Every line seemed equally likely, equally fatal. I never sorted them, never asked which ones mattered.
My friend Nilesh asked a week later, "So when do you start?" I said I was still researching risks.
That was February. It's October now. The four pages are still in my drawer, and I still haven't cooked a single tiffin.

The client demo was at ten the next morning. At six in the evening, in the small meeting room on the fourth floor, Dhruv handed out yellow slips.
"Imagine it's tomorrow at eleven and the demo went badly," he said. "Write down why. Don't sign it. Nobody talk yet."
The two senior developers wrote quickly and pushed their slips across. Mridul, who had joined three months ago and rarely spoke in meetings, wrote for a long time.
Dhruv read them aloud. The seniors had written "client asks for a feature we don't have" and "projector fails". Then Mridul's: "Dashboard takes forty seconds to load with real data. Login breaks if the client uses their office single sign-on."
The room went quiet. Nobody had tested either.
"Okay," Dhruv said. "Two things tonight. Mridul, can you show me the login problem first?"
Mridul nodded, cheeks a little pink.

Coaching centre note, Saturday 5 p.m.
Irawati was on time for the physics mock today, which surprised me. Her mother usually drops her, and I knew her mother was out of town this week.
At the break I asked how she got here. She explained it like a physics problem. "Getting across town felt impossible, so I broke it up. First, how to reach the main road bus stop. That's a ten-minute walk, fine. Then which bus. I asked the shop uncle and he said 42 goes near here. Then the fare. I checked I had coins."
She said none of the steps was hard on its own. Only the whole thing looked scary.
I've written the bus number and route on the centre's notice board for others without a lift.
— Gautam, physics faculty

passage:
Monday night
Big day. Papa's scooter broke down this morning and he said, sorry, no lift to coaching. My test was at four, across the whole city.
For ten minutes I just panicked. Then I remembered Sudha Ma'am saying, when a sum looks too big, split it.
So I did. Problem one: get to a bus stop. The one near the temple, fifteen minutes' walk. Solved. Problem two: which bus? I messaged my classmate Neha, she said 18A, then change to 7 at the market. Solved. Problem three: money. I had forty rupees in my pencil pouch. Enough. Solved.
It took an hour and ten minutes. I reached at 3.52, sweaty but there.
Sudha Ma'am saw me and smiled. I didn't tell her how scared I'd been.
Payal

qa.q: How long did the trip to coaching take?
qa.a: It took an hour and ten minutes.

qa.q: How can you tell Payal was scared when the lift fell through?
qa.a: Payal says the first ten minutes were spent just panicking, and later admits not telling Sudha Ma'am how scared it had felt.

qa.q: What else could Payal do before the next coaching day?
qa.a: Payal could write down the bus route and keep fare aside in advance, so a missed lift is not a panic next time.

qa.q: How might Sudha Ma'am see Payal arriving at 3.52?
qa.a: She sees a student who made it on time and is pleased, without knowing how hard it was, which is why she only smiles.

grounding: It shows a teenager with no lift breaking a trip across town into small subgoals: the stop, the bus numbers and the fare.
